source.display_title: 06/06/2026 - Gautam Bhatia x Andrew Musial  — Closed

setter.evidence: No setter is referenced anywhere and no suffix appears in the title. The prospect describes an inbound path from Trevor's own content — 'I watched the videos online', 'I've been watching a lot of his videos and that's obviously, that's why we're here' — and the only scheduling friction mentioned is 'It took a while to, I guess, get synced together'. The rep also introduces himself as the first point of contact: 'I'm the first point of contact.'

prospect.name: Gautam Bhatia
prospect.aka: gb — the speaker label changes at 00:04:25 when he gives up on his laptop camera and rejoins from his phone. Same person throughout.
prospect.location: Silicon Valley / Bay Area, California, USA (Pacific time). Originally from New Delhi, India; grew up in Dubai.
prospect.occupation: Semiconductor engineer and manager in Silicon Valley — around 20 years with the same organisation, manages and interviews people
prospect.family_status: Married. One daughter, Shania, aged one and a half. He and his wife describe themselves as 'older parents because they're in our forties'.
prospect.training_background: On and off through his thirties. Completed a triathlon at 30 — a one-mile swim, 30-mile bike and six-to-seven-mile run. Did P90X religiously for about two years through the COVID period, roughly 2020-2023, and gained noticeable muscle and strength. Since 2023 has effectively stopped: currently a couple of weekend workouts and maybe one weekday session, either isometric holds or the P90X 'core synergistics' routine, no resistance training and no focused cardio. Owns adjustable dumbbells he no longer uses and has already bought an adjustable Bowflex kettlebell up to 40 lb after watching Trevor's videos. Can now run about a mile to a mile and a half.
prospect.medical: Lower back ache developed over the last couple of years, attributed to prolonged sitting with poor posture and to months of carrying his daughter in a forward, slouched position. It comes and goes rather than being constant — worse at night and after standing for extended periods, which is why he abandoned a standing desk. Reports a weak core and self-diagnosed anterior pelvic tilt, which he explicitly believes needs correcting before he loads: 'that definitely needs something corrective before I start loading and trying to do things that are more in terms of building muscle.' Reports that leg work reproducibly injures his lower back — 'especially when I work on my legs, I end up invariably hurting my back, lower back... especially with P90X.' Very tight hips with limited rotation, and generally poor mobility. No heart condition, diabetes or blood pressure issues. Both parents are diabetic; his own sugar levels were normal at last check. Energy dips reliably after lunch.

signals: Lost clear ground to a hard season — work intensifying in 2023 plus a new baby — and names it: 'I've prioritized work over everything else last couple of years. And so, obviously, my body is telling me that I need to fix things.'
Wants a former self back and quantifies the loss precisely: a triathlon at 30 versus a mile and a half now. 'So there's a huge degradation that's happened.'
Carries visible regret and corrects himself when he hears his own excuses: 'So excuses, yes, maybe these are excuses. But I feel like that's how my brain was working.'

Driven by an accelerating-decline frame rather than by ambition: 'there's a certain ages where the aging effect starts accelerating... early forties to mid-40s is one acceleration point... I need to do something corrective here before it goes too far.'
NOT the_optimizer despite the income and job title — he is not currently fit, has back pain, has lost muscle and mobility, and is trying to recover a baseline rather than exceed one.

Overlays an unusually methodical buying style on the rebuilder profile: he asked for contactable customer references and framed it as professional practice, 'I interview people and I find them very compelling, but I always check references before I pull the trigger.'

goals.text: Be functional and hold on to strength and mobility as he ages, having noticed clear regression in his early forties
Be fit enough to ski, play tennis and swim with his daughter for the long haul as an older parent
Get rid of the lower back ache and the hip and joint stiffness
Fix his weak core and posture, including a self-suspected anterior pelvic tilt, so he can stand and work without pain
Get back to triathlon-level endurance — he swam a mile, biked 30 and ran six or seven at 30 years old
Lose excess body fat, though explicitly not focused on the scale — 'as long as I'm healthy, I feel like I'm comfortable with that'
Keep the regimen simple enough that he actually sticks to it — 'the only thing that's ever worked for me is a simple regimen'

pains.text: Lower back ache from prolonged sitting and from carrying his daughter, which reproducibly worsens when he trains legs and forced him to abandon a standing desk
Weak core and self-suspected anterior pelvic tilt that he believes must be corrected before he loads
Very tight hips with little rotation and generally poor mobility — cannot kick to any height
Work absorption has crowded out health for years — 'when you're like so absorbed into something it bothers you so much that you can't focus on anything else'
A 6am to 10:30pm day with a 40-minute commute each way and work resuming after dinner leaves no carved-out slot for training
Two decades of starting and stopping, with no mechanism that survives a busy period
Over-complicates his own approach — 'I try to over-complicate things, look at different kinds of videos, and do a lot of different things'
Under-eats through the day, drinks too little water and eats a carb-heavy delivered dinner at 7-7:30pm before working again
Energy and productivity fall away every afternoon, noticeably worse than in previous years
Believes he trained with poor form and no attention to mobility or recovery even when he was consistent

objections.raw_quote: I think the only thing I would say that might make me think about it, is if you tell me like, hey, Gautam, you've got to come in for three hours every day, and do XYZ... there is a certain level of time beyond which I'll be like, okay, I feel like I don't think I can add this much time every day, because it puts my life completely on pause
objections.rep_response: Answered directly and well. The rep led the training pillar with the time answer — three to four sessions a week at 30 to 40 minutes, plus five-to-fifteen-minute mobility protocols that fit between meetings — and tied it to the prospect's stated preference for morning training. Fully resolved; the prospect never raised time again except to check weekend scheduling.

objections.raw_quote: I've seen some of the testimonials on the website and I feel like it's great progress. But I felt like those people were at least fitter than me to begin with when they started. Are there examples or cases where people have come in with bad posture and some pain and they've managed to fix it?
objections.rep_response: Answered with an unevidenced assertion — 'I would say majority of our Our clients are people having pains and not having proper posture, desks, sitting at a desk all day. So I would say this is the majority of clients.' No case, no example, no name, no mechanism. The prospect accepted it and moved on, but nothing in the answer addressed his specific concern about loading a back that reliably fails under leg work.

objections.raw_quote: does this work well in a remote kind of communication, I guess, where you're not able to necessarily provide guidance in person, I guess?
objections.rep_response: Reframed rather than evidenced: 'this is the best next thing to actually having a trainer standing with you by your side', followed by a business-model argument that a personal trainer is incentivised to keep you dependent while 'Trevor's business model is different. He wants to set you up for life.' The prospect liked the framing — 'I like the fact that you guys teach a man to fish' — so it landed, but the underlying question of whether remote correction works for his posture was not answered.

objections.raw_quote: So in terms of just references, do you think there are references you could provide me as, you know, before I get into a program, I'd like to at least do my homework. Just the engineer in me likes to do the due diligence before committing to something that's really important to me.
objections.rep_response: The dominant objection of the call, unresolved across roughly fifteen minutes. The rep ran, in order: an isolate ('Is there anything coming up for you that's making you ask that?'), a reputation argument ('reputation is all we have... few bad reviews that go viral that destroy the business'), an unprompted 'I'm not AI. You're talking to a real human', a privacy policy ('we cannot and we don't actually reveal customers' personal details apart from those who agreed'), a second isolate, a hypothetical dismissal ('do you think that I would connect you with someone that wasn't 100% delighted'), a certainty reframe ('certainty only comes from action'), and finally a taunt — 'do you think that you are so... So unique, like a unicorn, that it wouldn't work for you, only for you, but it worked for over a thousand clients'. The prospect corrected him three separate times that this was procedure rather than doubt. It was ultimately not answered but bypassed, by inventing a one-month trial.

objections.raw_quote: In terms of his simplicity, but in terms of just committing to a six-month program and pulling the trigger for that, I feel like just the engineer in me always likes to verify things and make sure that this has been successful for people around me and people who have a similar lifestyle as me.
objections.rep_response: PROPOSED LABEL: 'commitment_duration'. The six-month term, not the price, was the barrier — 'it's a long time, and that's how I'm thinking about it'. The rep eventually addressed it directly and it is what closed the deal: he offered a one-month 'love it or leave it' at $1,200 with the remaining $4,800 due at month end. The prospect accepted almost immediately: 'I think that month duration is something that I think I can work with.'

offer.payment_plan_terms: A one-month 'love it or leave it' entry at $1,200 paid on the call, with $4,800 due at the end of the first month if he continues, totalling the standard $6,000 for six months. The rep framed it as exceptional: 'Because we don't do that. We like, we do that only in particular cases that someone like really needs to find out what is, what it's like.' The prospect restated the arithmetic and the rep confirmed it: 'So $4,800 comes in at the end of the first month, try to move forward.' Separately the rep restated the six-to-twelve upgrade term — 'you just top that up, that three missing K, that 3,000'. No refund was mentioned at any point; the $1,200 buys a month, it does not buy a money-back trial. A pause provision was also offered for injury or travel: 'if you would break your leg, something unpredictable, that you cannot work out. That's fine, too. We can just pause that.'

prospect_financials.disclosed: No financial constraint of any kind. He removed price from the conversation himself the moment it was presented — 'It's not, not about the, um, I'm not thinking about the money' — and later volunteered that he would pay more for confidence: 'if that means that there's a higher dollar commitment to getting that comfort level, I'm even willing to work with that.' He paid by credit card on the call without hesitation.

evidence: Payment was actually taken and verified on the call, so the close rule was not needed. Rep: 'I'll send you the link for the six months. No, that's one month. I'll put it in the chat. Did you get it?' — 'Got it. Yep, yep, got it.' — 'Let me know when you're done with that so I can check it on my end.' — 'Yeah, it's done.' — 'Okay, cool.'

Trevor onboarding call booked live for Monday the 15th at 10:15 Pacific, with the calendar confirmation verified as received: 'you should get a confirmation email to your email right now for the meeting' — 'Yep. I got it.'
Explicit commitment: 'All right. Let's move forward. This is good.'
COUNTER-EVIDENCE on the size of the win: only $1,200 was collected. The remaining $4,800 is genuinely optional under the love-it-or-leave-it structure and should not be booked as contract value.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE on completeness: the agreement email never arrived and was never signed. The rep checked with a VA on Slack and relayed 'the most important thing is that I got you on the call with Trevor, and I will just let know Angelo from Trevor's team... So he will send you that manually, probably on Monday.' The client has paid with no signed terms in hand.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE on retention risk: the reference objection was never actually resolved, only bypassed, and the prospect said plainly 'I'll just go look at the testimonials and I'll make my mind up based on that.' He is buying a month specifically to verify what he could not verify beforehand.
outcome.cash_collection_basis: one_month_love_it_or_leave_it_only — the further $4,800 is optional at month end and is not committed contract value
outcome.next_step: Trevor onboarding call Monday 15 June, 10:15 Pacific. Angelo on Trevor's admin side to send the agreement manually on Monday, plus the Skool community invitation, the onboarding form and app access. Rep gave his personal WhatsApp number.

notable.note: The cleanest ICP fit in this batch, with no price objection whatsoever, closed for $1,200 instead of $6,000. The blocker was never money — he said so twice and offered to pay more for confidence — it was that he wanted to speak to a reference before committing six months, which is exactly how he says he hires people. The company has no referenceable clients, the script has no play for the request, and after fifteen minutes of reframing a rational due-diligence request as fear and comfort-seeking, including asking whether he thought he was 'a unicorn', the rep bought his way out with an off-policy monthly tier. Two other things a principal should see. He disclosed that leg work reliably injures his lower back and that he believes his pelvic tilt needs correcting before he loads, and was sold loaded kettlebell training with a lay diagnosis and no clinical clearance — and the rep then confirmed Trevor performs no physical assessment at all: 'what kind of shape I am in, does he need to look at that or no? No, no, no, no.' And the agreement email failed to send, with the VA's guidance being that booking the Trevor call mattered more.

quality.notes: Systematic inversion through the middle and late call, plus a genuine mid-call identity change. The prospect starts as 'Gautam Bhatia' and becomes 'gb' at 00:04:25 when he abandons his laptop camera and rejoins from his phone; both labels are the same person, and for a period the rep reports seeing two of him in the room. From roughly 00:41:31 onward the labels invert almost wholesale during the pillar pitch — the entire training-and-mobility delivery opening 'So the first thing that we're going to focus on is your training and your mobility' is labelled gb but is unmistakably the rep, and the same pattern recurs at 00:54:14, 00:59:03, 01:01:00, 01:21:03 and through the whole booking sequence after 01:32:04. Conversely long prospect passages appear under the rep's label, including the reference-checking argument at 01:07:52 and the P90X comparison at 01:19:00. There is also a verbatim duplicated block: the exchange about the missing agreement email at 01:39:44-01:39:53 is repeated word for word at 01:40:10-01:40:51. Roles resolved from content throughout; timestamps reliable. The rep's phone number readback is also inconsistent, given as 970-215-6316 at 01:37:01 and as 970-215-663-16 at 01:46:05.
